items.question: How do you see foundation models changing the role of humans in data annotation?
items.object: The shift from conventional annotation to agentic labeling
items.answer: What we've been doing as annotation, just blindly sending everything out for labeling, is not the future. We're seeing foundation models come along that could indeed actually replace a lot of those typical case human labels. So if what was annotation 1.0, blind send me data and get me labels, annotation 2.0 might only be human answers questions asked by the agent, if you will, agentic labeling or something like that. To me, we're on that timeline, and we're probably somewhere in the middle of it.

items.question: Why did you see a need for more analysis tooling in computer vision?
items.object: Analysis tooling for developing computer vision models and data sets together
items.answer: Most of my work focuses on high level computer vision, video understanding, vision language, relationship between the physical world and vision, and so on. And through that work at the University of Michigan, I realized that there was a huge need for more analysis tooling to help support the code development of models and data sets together. And ultimately, that's given me rise to the last five or so years of my life at Voxel51 and the university together.

items.question: How has your understanding of real-world computer vision development shaped your goals for Voxel51's 51 software?
items.object: Joint dataset and model development and the purpose of Voxel51's 51 software
items.answer: What we've learned over the years generally is, you don't just get data dropped into your lap like a student does in my computer vision class, right, and then you have to train the model. Real world life in the real world is making the data set alongside making the model and really understanding how these things coincide together. And so that's ultimately why we released 51, which is the name of our primary software. It's both commercial and open source, so open source for single users, local data, local compute. That's really how we got started in 2019 when we began this direction toward dev tool. We released it open source both in the computer vision community and the machine learning community. And it's become a pretty widely adopted tool for everyday usage. Our initial charge was, for the first three things someone does when they're starting a new computer vision project, pip install 51 should be one of those things, one of those first three things.

items.question: How do you think 51 should fit into a computer vision user's way of working?
items.object: 51's flexible software design
items.answer: I think 51's a pretty flexible piece of software. It's not intended to tell you how to do your work or what to do. Think of it kind of like a set of building blocks, and if you want some annotation or you want model performance analysis or you just want to visualize your embeddings or whatever, it can kind of do all these different pieces for you. So, we do have a pretty broad user base.

items.question: How did you arrive at 51's early emphasis on flexible model analysis rather than direct annotation?
items.object: 51's early decision to emphasize analysis and flexibility instead of direct annotation
items.answer: I have personally fallen prey to that direction as well. When I was a postdoc at UCLA, I built my own 3D—I was working in 3D medical imaging, so there was no 3D medical image annotation tool out there, so I built my own one at the time. In fact, I think that notion was so prevalent in our strategic thinking early on that within 51, from the very beginning, we explicitly did not support annotation directly. So in order to annotate in 51, we provided integrations with common annotation tools like C and Label Studio, Labelbox, other annotation tools, mostly because there were so many of them out there, and we felt like it was going to be hard to distinguish any new tool like ours from another tool that was already out there. We really wanted to emphasize the notion at the very core of what we did is, you train, you get some data and you train a model, and then it doesn't work as well as you think. So you're like, what do I do next? Let me get more data and let me turn—you kind of iterate this loop, and we inject 51 into the middle of that as the analysis work, right? So kind of like turning the lights on in a dark hallway, right? It's like you get some data, train some models, then you do analysis within 51, and then you kind of repeat this loop. And that's why we made it flexible, though, because that loop is very team specific. In fact, I used to quip, for every 100 machine learning engineers out there, there are 10,000 ways of working, because everyone has their own way of doing things, really.

items.question: Why do you continue to value integrations with external annotation tools as 51 gains its own annotation capabilities?
items.object: 51's continued integration with external annotation tools
items.answer: We still maintain the integrations with other annotation tools. Now, even though you can annotate within 51 through this auto-labeling stuff, and actually, coming out in the summer, you will be able to do some classical annotation within 51. But we still integrate with all the other tools out there. And I think it's primarily because 51 has become a little bit of a Rosetta Stone for visual data formats. items.question: Why do you see the human expert as essential to diagnosing a computer vision model’s failure modes?
items.object: Human expertise in diagnosing computer vision model failures
items.answer: So one key use case for that is, you've a data set, you have a model. Obviously, it doesn't perform perfectly. So what can you do? One question you might want to ask is, what are the corner cases? Where is it performing poorly? And are there commonalities or is there structure to that lack of performance? So we have capabilities in the system to, for example, compute what we call hardness or mistakenness, that take your model logits on the data and manipulate them in certain ways to then provide to you clusters of outputs that you can then visually analyze. Because in our view, the human expert, like the actual domain expert or the MLE in the loop, is the one who is the only one who really can make the decision. You know, we're training a pedestrian avoidance algorithm, and it turns out there's very few examples of suburban parking lots for some reason. Only the human really is going to identify that that was the failure mode of the problem.

items.question: Why do you consider interactive embedding visualization important for cleaning a computer vision data set?
items.object: Interactive embedding visualization for cleaning computer vision data
items.answer: Another analysis we use is visualization of embeddings. So you can compute your embeddings either with a 51-approved embedding model, or you kind of bring your own embedding model for that. And then you can visually interact in the app to find situations for mislabels on your actual data set, right? So you visualize your embeddings, you can project the class labels on those embeddings, and ultimately we'll see, well, this big mass of red labels here with some blue labels in them. Let me see what those blue labels are. So let me turn the red mask off, the red label off, and then I can get a view only into those blue labels. So it's really this notion of interactive analysis that is imperative to cleaning up your data and finding corner cases where you might then need to add more labels for the task.

items.question: How do you understand the forces behind the shift toward automated labeling in computer vision?
items.object: The shift toward automated labeling in computer vision
items.answer: Yeah, I think I'd be lying if I told you in 2018, when we were first starting the company, or 2007, when I started as faculty, I was going to predict, like, oh wait, we're not going to need labeling anymore. That couldn't be true, but it's not necessarily strictly a function of just recent development. About maybe two years ago, we began to see a shift in the types of conversations we would have with users of 51, where they were going from, like, I'm strictly sending all of my data to humans to annotate and spending, just say round number, I'm spending a million dollars on this, and then I'm getting it back, and instead of being able to use it all, I'm finding out that actually I can only use 10% of it or 20%, which dollars for dollars means they're throwing away a significant amount of money.

items.question: Why do you see selecting the right data for annotation as a harder problem than correcting mislabels?

Like data, it's easy to find typical plus or minus a couple sigma cases, but what really matters is finding data along the decision boundaries. And that's hard to do if you don't know what the decision boundaries are, right? So the conversation shifted over into that direction. items.question: What were you trying to challenge with your blog post “Annotation Is Dead”?
items.object: The argument behind his blog post “Annotation Is Dead”
items.answer: So I wrote a blog maybe January of 2024 with the title “Annotation Is Dead.” It was intended to start this conversation generally around, should we really be doing what we've been doing? It wasn't so much that no one's going to need annotated data. Obviously it's a well-oiled machine. We know how supervised machine learning works. We can measure somewhat predictable performance, things like that, right? But it was really intended to catalyze this notion that, wait a second, what we've been doing as annotation, just blindly sending everything out for labeling, is not the future. The future cannot be that way. It just so happened that we also were seeing at that time foundation models come along that could indeed actually replace a lot of those typical case human labels, and so you don't even need to do that anymore.

items.question: How do you envision the transition toward what you call annotation 2.0?
items.object: Annotation 2.0 and agentic labeling
items.answer: So if what was annotation maybe we call that annotation 1.0, and annotation 2.0 is like, there's never blind send me data and get me labels. Annotation 2.0 might only be a human answers questions asked by the agent, if you will, agentic labeling or something like that. To me, we're on that timeline, and we're probably somewhere in the middle of it. Not just we, like Voxel51, but I think the community generally. We're moving down the line of, okay, we can expect to get decent labels for common classes. What can we expect for less common classes? Or, I have an automotive scenario, can you predict my model performance without actually labeling the data beforehand? Things like that. And I think we're right squarely in the middle, moving in the direction of fewer just, “Here's the media, give me the metadata,” toward more like, “I think this is a teddy bear. Is this really a teddy bear?” These are not technically speaking new directions. People in the community of machine learning and computer vision have been looking at this for at least a decade or two. Semi-supervised learning is not new. Active learning is not new. But I think what we're seeing is that with the creation of these semantically enriched foundation models and embedding spaces, there's more of an underlying structure to the way data is represented in those embedding spaces that we need to crunch on and understand more, so that we can then go and do a better job of asking the right questions.

items.question: How do you think semantically enriched embedding spaces help us measure uncertainty in computer vision models?
items.object: Estimating uncertainty and classification difficulty using semantically enriched embedding spaces
items.answer: I do think uncertainty is at the core of a lot of this discussion. In some sense, if we really want a true measure of uncertainty, like a classical P of X type uncertainty, I still don't think we're quite there yet. We haven't made much progress, right? We still don't really know how to do that. But there is enough structure in these embedding spaces that we can start to even leverage some classical ideas. For example, we have a tech report that we've been working on that is able to take a classification problem and embed it using these contemporary foundation model embeddings. So take a classic perceptual embedding like ResNet 18, concatenate that with a CLIP embedding space, and model within that space. And the problem we set out to ask is, can we measure the difficulty, the expected classification difficulty, in that space without training the downstream classifier? Assuming, say, we only had labels on a small subset of the data, like 100 samples per class, for example. And we use very simple shallow autoencoders, like two, three layer autoencoders. They're trainable in seconds per class. And if you take ratios of reconstruction errors, which is a measure of uncertainty to some degree, there are certain classes of those ratios that correlate very strongly with downstream classifier performance, had you trained a full classifier on the whole data set. So that's what leads me to say that this is evidence, if you will, that there seems to be some structure in these more semantically enriched embedding spaces that, even though we still don't have the right machinery to go and fully compute uncertainty, we at least can get, using the term loosely, kind of like marginal uncertainty in that space.

items.question: How do you understand the limitations of your fixed-embedding modeling approach when it comes to rare cases in a data set?
items.object: Rare cases and decision boundaries in fixed-embedding modeling
items.answer: There are no assumptions that we know that they occur in the data set, but we also can't deduce them. There's sort of no way to figure those out, right? Those are essentially the Bayes risk or the Bayes uncertainty, right? I guess, essentially, what we've observed is that the decision boundary is always going to be the challenge here, right? And since we're not, in that work, for example, updating the embedding at all, we don't modulate the embedding to try to pull them apart. If indeed a data set is dominated by those rare cases that are hard to disentangle from the truth, then it would be kryptonite for this modeling that we did. But in typical situations, the mean is the mean, right? Typical samples are typical samples.

items.question: What is your intuition about how moving toward internet-scale data sets affects the behavior that dominates the data?
items.object: Internet-scale data sets and the dominance of mean behavior
items.answer: What I'd like to see, though, and we haven't done this, is—I’ve been hearing this notion of internet scale data sets or real scale data sets coming up in the vision community a lot in the last couple years. I still don't have a great sense for how to quantify what is an internet scale data set versus a canned off-the-shelf data set. But my intuition says that the closer we get to large scale internet scale data sets, the more the mean behavior is going to dominate. And I think that's critical.

items.question: What do you see as the key challenges in making auto-labeling useful when your models may already handle much of the data well?
items.object: The value and challenges of auto-labeling
items.answer: That is the observation I think many of us are making collectively, right? Why am I spending this money on things that I'm pretty sure even my own models may do well with already? And I think the challenge is—I think there are two key challenges, really. One is, how can we build a model of predictability, using the term model loosely here? How much of that auto-labeling can I expect to be useful? And I think that's a key challenge. And then another one is, given that I've just auto-labeled things, how do I minimize the human work needed to do QA on the output of that?

items.question: Why did you choose such a simple experimental setup for your report “Auto-Labeling Data for Object Detection”?
items.object: The experimental setup in the report “Auto-Labeling Data for Object Detection”
items.answer:
I think this initial report and our initial work in it is probably the simplest setup that you can imagine, simply because, you know, I've been around for some time, and I think simple works. We need to get in the simplest case before we can talk about more complex settings. So basically, the assumptions are you have a foundation model that is relevant to the domain you're operating in, general natural images, whatever, and then you have a VLM in particular. I guess a VLM in particular because we do prompt it with labels. I mean, the data sets we work with are VOC, COCO, BDD, and LVIS. So all of our prompts were pretty simple. That's why I'm sort of hesitating at VLM in the sense that the foundation models we used are like YOLO-World, YOLOE, Grounding DINO, concretely. So they're not really VLMs, but more generally speaking, you could say VLM. And you have a large corpus of unlabeled data, basically, right?

The idea is, what would you have done in annotation 1.0? You would have sent all of those images to humans to label. You would have taken the output from them and trained your model, your object detector in this case, and then computed some validation performance on a holdout set that was part of those annotations as well. In our auto-labeling scenario, take the same unlabeled data, take a foundation model, generate those labels, auto-labels, and similarly train an apples-to-apples sort of object detector. We use RT-DETR, YOLO, YOLO11, I think, and then compute the same validation performance. We wanted to make it as apples to apples. There's nothing special about the domain or the use case or what have you, aside from the fact that we're only doing object detection.

Other assumptions we made are only one foundation model for input. There's no voting. There was some recent work, like the Florence 2 model at CVPR, I think 24. They had this interesting notion of a data engine where they're weighting over multiple foundation model outputs. We don't do any of that. Again, simplest case here. We wanted to assess, given these simple settings, what is the cost comparison in terms of money and time? How well do the auto-labels match human labels? And how well do the downstream object detectors match object detectors that were trained on those human labels? Those really were the three things.

I should say, concretely, there's no new architecture here. There's no technical contribution that way. The only parameter we vary is the threshold on the model confidence per object label, per object auto-label. We wanted to keep it as simple as possible, just because I think there's a lot that we could do downstream in the future, but if we don't have a good baseline—and I think concretely, we approach it this way not just because it's important to do things simple first, but we weren't aware of a baseline that actually did this experiment that compares cost to ultimate gain in downstream performance or what have you. So that's the way we set it up.

items.question: How did you think about the choice of downstream model architectures in your auto-labeling experiments?
items.object: Choice of downstream model architectures in the auto-labeling experiments
items.answer: Downstream models that we trained were different sizes of YOLO11. So YOLO11 N, S, M, L, and X varies from 2.6 million to 57 million parameters, and then RT-DETR, which has 33 million parameters. In some sense, we wanted to take one model architecture, vary its capacity, and then a completely different model architecture at roughly the mean capacity of the first one, is the way I would think about those.

items.question: How do you think about the cost comparison between human labeling and model-generated labeling in your research?
items.object: The cost comparison between human labeling and model-generated labeling
items.answer: We did this on a box of six GPUs, six L40Ss, and it took about a month, so whatever that cost is. But that's the full research experiment, not the cost analysis. So it's six orders of magnitude more expensive to have humans label than have models label. That's expected, so it's not surprising that the cost is greatly different, $124,000 to a dollar, right? That's expected, but I think quantifying it is still something that we weren't aware someone had done, right? So I think even putting a pin in the ground is important to do in science. Ultimately, it only matters if the labels are good.

items.question: How do you assess the value of the time and cost savings from automated data labeling?
items.object: The value of automated data labeling’s time and cost savings
items.answer: So we estimate that it would take about 6,000 hours of humans to label these four data sets. And this is based on a paper from Kristen Groman's group in, I think, ICCB 2017 or 2019, where they were measuring the value of labeling or the cost of labeling. So 6,000 hours to one hour to one and a quarter hours, about four orders of magnitude difference there as well. So you can do it fast and you can do it cheaply, but does it work? Does it matter?
quotes: So we estimate that it would take about 6,000 hours of humans to label these four data sets. And this is based on a paper from Kristen Groman's group in, I think, ICCB 2017 or 2019, where they were measuring the value of labeling or the cost of labeling.

items.question: How do you view human annotations as a gold standard for evaluating automatic image labels?
items.object: Human annotations as a gold standard for evaluating automatic image labels
items.answer: We looked at how well we can reproduce the human labels, which is important, right? Just as a measure of they are in some sense a gold standard, although they're not a perfect gold standard. For example, one of the data sets has an image of donuts and these two trays of donuts in the image. I actually forget which data set it comes from, maybe LVIS. In the human labels, it's a mess, actually. If there are something like six dozen donuts per tray across both of them, roughly, that's probably about what it is, maybe a little less than that, four dozen. Humans sometimes—this is real data, right—they will only label three of the donuts, a handful of the donuts, right? This stuff is tedious. Similarly, they might group together six donuts as one donut, and one example we have is the whole entire tray, essentially the whole image of donuts, is labeled as donuts, which is complete ontological failure of the domain, right? Whereas the auto-labels, okay, they miss some of the donuts, but it doesn't make the egregious error of grouping them together and so on. So that was a great finding, I guess.

items.question: How do you assess the practical importance of confidence thresholds when using foundation models for auto-labeling?
items.object: Confidence thresholds and the practical reliability of auto-labeling foundation models
items.answer: If you do assume that human labels are perfect, or are the gold standard, we have found that performance does vary drastically based on the configuration. In this case, it's essentially what confidence threshold you use. It's a “we keep this label or not” basically. That confidence threshold is coming straight from the model, YOLO or what have you, without doing any calibration at all. So we just took it as is, black box. We do notice that Grounding DINO has the greatest variation in performance of the three foundation models, whereas YOLO-World and YOLOE are—maybe at the boundaries of the curve it does fall off pretty drastically, but from confidence 0.3 to 0.7 it's a pretty flat, plateaued performance in terms of F1 to the human labeling. So that's a good finding, right? In some sense, for each of the three foundation models we used, if you're able to find the right confidence threshold, you can essentially get almost perfect F1 score. Maybe that's a little bit reaching. You can get very good, let's say comparable F1 score to make it usable. The challenge is, in practice, you don't necessarily have—you can't calibrate that well. You'll have to get some data labeled to do your calibration of your confidence and then go and hope that that extrapolates to the rest of the data set.

items.question: Why do you consider downstream model performance the right measure of auto-labeling quality?
items.object: Downstream model performance as the measure of auto-labeling quality
items.answer: The challenge is, in practice, you can't calibrate that well. You'll have to get some data labeled to do your calibration of your confidence and then go and hope that that extrapolates to the rest of the data set. So we really think the right measure is the other axis that we measured, which was: take the auto-labels and measure their downstream model performance. So this is where we train the 445 models and do the analysis there. And what we found is that in all cases for each of the three variants of foundation model across all four data sets, we can get relative numbers in the 80s and 90s performance of whatever. Say YOLO11S human performance is 60% accuracy; an auto-labeled YOLO11S can get 55% performance or something like that. Very close performance. Interestingly, there are some interesting findings here. One is that if you're willing to save the money you would have spent on annotation and instead train a bigger model for compute and spend that money over time, you can, apples to apples, actually outperform the smaller model. YOLO11S has 9 million parameters; YOLO11N has 2.6 million parameters. If you're willing to train the YOLO11S, you can outperform the YOLO11N in many of the results we have as well, which is a cool result, I think. But even more interestingly, the best downstream model performance comes for confidence thresholds filtering in and out the auto-labels that are not aligned with the top F1 performance.

items.question: How do you interpret the finding that lowering the confidence threshold for auto-labels improves downstream object detector performance?
items.object: Low confidence thresholds and noisy auto-labels for training object detectors
items.answer: What we found is that lowering your confidence threshold to somewhat egregiously low numbers like 0.12, where you will have noisy outputs in the auto-labels, ultimately maps to better downstream performance. And I thought this was really exciting. It's not necessarily super counterintuitive, but also consistent with other results we're seeing recently, like there was a paper within the past couple weeks about RL fine-tuning. It doesn't really matter what the answers are. The general idea is consistent with machine learning just seems to perform better when there's the right amount of noise, like dropout and all these other things that we've done to create noise when we're training models. So from that perspective, maybe not surprising, but counterintuitive.

items.question: What do you see as the significance of your report on using foundation models for auto-labeling?
items.object: The significance of the report on foundation models for auto-labeling
items.answer: I think it's just another chip, or another tile in the mosaic of messaging around machine learning. Models need data, and the data does not have to be perfect, but more is better than—more is better than better, in some sense. I don't have the right mantra yet, but it's indeed pointing in that direction. And I think, in some sense, what I hope for this particular report is that it gets recognized in the community as rather concrete and up-to-date evidence for not only that counterintuitive nature, but a way of measuring how well these contemporary foundation models perform in the context of auto-labeling.

items.question: How do you understand the limits of zero-shot auto-labeling based on the datasets you tested?
items.object: The limits of zero-shot auto-labeling on out-of-domain classes
items.answer: These data sets that we've used in this experiment are mostly, let's say, in-domain data sets for the foundation models we used. VOC, COCO, even BDD—most or all of the classes in those three data sets are at least covered in some way or another in the training data for the foundation models that were used. The exact images were not used, but the concepts were there. LVIS, I think, is a little bit different, where it has something like 1,200 classes, and we incorporated LVIS to measure limitations of this case, where we find clearly if there are no labels predicted, then downstream object detector performance is not going to be there. So a limitation of this notion of auto-labeling is how do you handle the decision boundary classes or complex classes that are out of domain?

items.question: How do you envision verified auto-labeling making human review manageable?
items.object: Verified auto-labeling with selective human review
items.answer: I think the key nugget here is being able to identify either automatically or semi-automatically, with a human in the loop, when these auto-labels should be accepted and when they should be rejected. The way I think Voxel51 is going to be doing it within 51 is this notion of what we're calling verified auto-labeling. You generate your auto-labels, and it's still the onus is on the human, whether or not it's a QA person that you're paying from outside the company or a team member, an actual trained MLE. Someone really should be saying yes, no, yes, no, yes, no, but it's a problem if they have to do that for every image. Our approach, or what we think will work, and we're still working on this admittedly, is being able to identify what we're thinking of as green, yellow, and red light. Think of it like a stoplight. Clearly these samples are in-cluster, in-class, right? They don't vary at all from the mean of the cluster, whether or not that's measured with the shallow autoencoder model I talked about earlier or some other—there probably are dozens of ways of doing that as long as you can do it fast and effectively. And similarly, the red light: these cases are clearly at the decision boundary. We aren't confident about these; we don't know what they are. So let's just throw away those. And then the challenge is the yellow, the cases in the middle. Are there cases where it's unclear if it's a decision boundary problem, like the child near the stop sign example you gave earlier, or if it's a mislabel from the auto-label or something like that? So let's have humans look at that. Ultimately, that's the way we're approaching the problem. Humans are still needed to verify. If you can minimize that work and quantify and predictably quantify how much work there would be, I think that's when we get to annotation next version of annotation, whether it's 1.5 or 2.0 or whatever.

items.question: How would you evaluate how well auto-labeling works in domains outside the foundation models' training domain?
items.object: Evaluating auto-labeling in out-of-distribution domains
items.answer: I don't have a great answer. I mean, we just haven't measured it, really. I think that's something we want to do. One way that we would measure that is, the first step we probably would do—and I'd be glad if someone else who's listening does this work before us. It's fine. This is not a competition, it's a cooperation, right? I would take a data set domain like medical imaging, for which there are in-domain foundation models, and then use out-of-domain foundation models like the ones we've used here as well as those in-domain ones.

I still don't think the current semantically enriched embedding spaces we have today are sufficiently compositional. But that's one direction of complexity.

items.question: What makes manufacturing defects a difficult domain for you to assess auto-labeling performance in?
items.object: Auto-labeling manufacturing defects
items.answer: One of our customers is looking at that notion, how do we find defects in production of glass, for example, or microchip type things? The way I joke about that problem is, in some sense, the way things can go well in terms of performance and building things on manufacturing lines are very few. It's correct or it's not correct, it's right. Whereas the way things can go wrong is this really massive and hard to predict space. I don't have a great answer for how we would assess this auto-labeling of that domain.

items.question: How do you envision the future of annotation and dataset building?
items.object: Embedding space agents as the future of dataset building
items.answer: In general, though, I think the way I envision the future of annotation, or data set building really, is we will have agents, almost like embedding space agents, who are trained, whether or not it's with RL, I don't know, but we'll train to be asking the domain experts when they're not sure directly. items.question: How do you envision an agentic approach to human-in-the-loop annotation going beyond sending low-certainty images to a user for review?
items.object: Agentic approaches to human-in-the-loop annotation
items.answer: I don't know. We're collectively overusing the term agent or the notion of agent right now. But I am thinking of it in the context of a human-in-the-loop UX, for sure. items.question: How do you view the prospects for putting methods that reduce human labeling for computer vision into practice?
items.object: Practical adoption of methods that reduce human labeling for computer vision
items.answer: I mean, I am really excited about how to bring this into practice. I see a lot of papers that try to do some form of this, or the whole world of semi-supervised ML. These are not really new ideas. Yet I still don't hear people singing from the mountaintops that, “Oh look, I don't need humans anymore for labeling this,” and, “My need for human labeling is 10% as it was last year.” So either they've discovered it and they're not talking about it, which is a possibility, or it's still just in this experimental stage. And I am really excited about the impact that these types of results or these types of systems will have in practice. I think we all want to see better AI models or better vision models being trained and being deployed, and I'm just hoping that this is one way in that direction for practical attack.

items.question: What research direction excites you about providing guarantees for computer vision systems that minimize human labeling?
items.object: Performance guarantees for computer vision systems that minimize human labeling
items.answer: I think from a near-term technical or more researchy direction, that notion of how you minimize human work but still provide some guarantees on it—there's a whole area in controls and other spaces in engineering that have mechanisms for measuring those types of uncertainties or performance guarantees and so on. We just haven't done that in our space. And I think as the field matures, we will need to mature the types of guarantees that we can offer in the space. So I'm pretty excited about that direction as well.

items.question: How do you view the use of VLMs and LLMs to generate synthetic datasets?
items.object: Using VLMs and LLMs to generate synthetic datasets
items.answer: I'm not an expert in the language domain specifically. I think there probably are similarities, but I think there are also interesting differences. I guess first of all, I'm a little worried about using VLMs or LLMs to generate synthetic data sets because they assume knowledge of the underlying embedding space, or the manifolds in that space, and we already know that we don't have full understanding. Those manifolds are not yet sufficiently well defined necessarily. And I guess evidence to that point, even in the text domain, is that although we see LLMs being used to generate data sets and so on, many annotation companies have left the vision space and moved into the text space because of the greater demand for more human expertise. And I think, why is that happening? Because there's this rich semantic structure in language that is sometimes hard to tease out. And I think there's still some learning to be done there. Whether or not it's to strictly—when we get to trillions of tokens, that will be enough, I don't know. I'll just shrug my shoulders at that. I don't really know. Maybe we need a different model. I'm not sure.

items.question: How do you think semantic ambiguity in computer vision compares with semantic ambiguity in language?
items.object: Semantic ambiguity in computer vision compared with language
items.answer: In the visual domain, the types of ambiguities you can find, those types of semantic ambiguities, frankly, I think are less. I don't want to be on record as saying computer vision is easier than NLP. Most of my colleagues would shoot me for saying that. But I think it's easier in some ways and harder in other ways, is a simple way to put it. There are some visual semantic ambiguities, like donut hole. I gave this in a talk at CVPR a decade ago or something like that. What's a donut hole? Is a donut hole actually the gap, the part of the doughnut that's missing, or is a donut hole the pop or whatever, the actual thing that came out of there? Until you've seen some examples, you don't necessarily know what that concept means. So there are certain ambiguities in the visual world like that. And it's just the visual world is much higher dimension and very complex to process. You could even argue that that's not actually a visual ambiguity, but a linguistic ambiguity.

items.question: How do you think about what makes visual perception a hard research problem?
items.object: Visual perception as a research problem
items.answer: We perceive to have some semantic grounding of what we perceive. And I think that's the bridge that makes it hard. Whereas I think the visual world is hard in other ways, right? The way shadows are created or the way reflections happen, or even my eyeglasses, for example, are highly reflective. In fact, I have a new pair waiting at the optometrist because it has that problem. Aspects like this, right? So anyway, good to be in research in these problem spaces these days because it's such a rich environment.
